<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, Rep. Adelita S. Grijalva>: INTRODUCTION
H.R. 8781, the Title IX Clarification Act of 2026, introduced by Rep. Jodey Arrington (R-TX), amends title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972 (Title IX) to ``clarify'' the definition of ``sex'' and to add definitions of ``female'' and ``male'' to the statute. The Majority claims this bill is needed to provide clarity in the face of legal ambiguity. Such ambiguity as to the definition of sex does not exist as a legal matter, as attested by recent Supreme Court decisions.\1\ H.R. 8781 is instead an attempt to write transgender students out of the law and deny them protection from discrimination based on their gender identity.
\1\Infra text accompanying notes 14-16.
TRANS-EXCLUSIONARY POLICIES ARE THE COIN OF THE MAJORITY'S REALM
Less than one percent of the U.S. population identifies as transgender.\2\ However, so far in the 119th Congress, the Committee has had no less than six hearings where the subject of gender identity in education has been discussed.\3\ H.R. 8781 is at least the sixth bill the Committee has either marked up or managed on the House floor of this Congress that involves gender identity in some fashion.\4\ This fixation comes at the expense of many issues in the Committee's jurisdiction that Americans want Congress to address such as ensuring that employers pay wages that keep up with the cost of basic necessities, expanding access to affordable child care, or expanding access to paid family and medical leave.\5\

H.R. 8781 MARS TITLE IX'S ANTI-DISCRIMINATORY LEGACY
Title IX states ``No person in the United States shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance ...''\6\ It is hard to overstate the transformational effect Title IX has had on American society. In its over 50-year history, Title IX has created opportunities for millions of women and girls to participate in sports at the high school and college levels. By 2016, two in every five girls in the United States played sports.\7\ Further, while the public may recognize the law's impact on sports primarily, Title IX prohibits sex discrimination in all vestiges of education; it has helped secure advancements for women in academic and career fields traditionally dominated by men and provided procedural and substantive rights for victims of sex discrimination, sex harassment and sexual assault in educational settings, irrespective of their gender.\8\
\6\20 U.S.C. Sec.  1681(a).
\7\Women's Sport Foundation, Title IX and the Rise of Female Athletes in America, (Sept. 2, 2016) https:// www.womenssportsfoundation.org/education/title-ix-and-the-rise-of-female-athletes-in-america/.
\8\Women's Sports Foundation, 50 Years of Title IX: We're Not Done Yet 7, 2021 https://www.womenssportsfoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/ 2022/05/Title-IX-at-50-Report-FINALC-v2-.pdf (``Pathways once closed or significantly inaccessible to women have opened as Title IX created greater access to academic pursuits leading to careers in an array of occupations for women, including but not limited to astronauts, athletes, carpenters, chief executive officers, construction workers, doctors, engineers, entrepreneurs, farmers, filmmakers, firefighters, football coaches, investors, journalists, lawyers, musicians, police officers, military personnel, rock stars, Supreme Court justices, and television news anchors.''); U.S. Dep't of Educ., Title IX and Sex Discrimination, last reviewed Jan. 30, 2026, https://www.ed.gov/laws-and-policy/civil-rights-laws/title-ix-and-sex-discrimination.
In recent years, Title IX has been discussed in the context of the right of transgender women to participate in sports consistent with their gender identity. The question as to whether ``sex'' in the context of Title IX includes sexual orientation and/or gender identity has been the subject of court cases, federal legislation, and administrative regulation. A version of these questions came before the Supreme Court this year in two cases heard concurrently, B.P.J. v. West Virginia, and Little v. Hecox. The very specific questions before the Court were whether, under Title IX and the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, schools may maintain women's and girls' sports teams for cisgender females, i.e., whether schools can determine eligibility for female sports based on sex assigned at birth.\9\
\9\B.P.J. v. West Virginia No. 24-43, slip op. at 2 (U.S., June 30, 2026).
The Court held 9-0 that Title IX allows schools to provide separate women's and men's sports teams defined by biological sex, and a state can limit participation based on biological sex at birth.\10\ Title IX and the Javits Amendment\11\ create a regulatory scheme that provides for separate teams for men and women because of the biological differences between the sexes. Title IX regulations authorize, ``separate women's and girls' teams in sports when the teams are `based upon competitive skill or the activity involved is a contact sport.'''\12\ The Court concluded it was reasonable at the time of Title IX's passage to separate sports teams based on ``sex'', which all parties before the Court agreed at the time of the law's writing, meant biological sex at birth. Because the law and amendments recognize in the sports context a reasonable distinction between the biological sexes, the Court held it is not discrimination on the basis of sex under Title IX to limit participation on sports teams based on biological sex at birth.\13\
\10\Id. at 9-12. When describing the Court's holding and rationale or quoting from H.R. 8781, we use the term the Court and the bill use-- biological sex--rather than the preferred ``sex assigned at birth''. National SOGIE Ctr., Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity & Expression Glossary of Terms, https://sogiecenter.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/ SOGIE-Glossary-Final.pdf (last visited Aug. 30, 2026).
\11\Much of the impact of Title IX in sports comes not from the law itself but the regulations promulgated under it. These were the result of the Javits Amendment, which directed the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare (the predecessor to the Department of Education) to promulgate ``reasonable (regulatory) provisions considering the nature of particular sports''' in intercollegiate athletics.'' U.S. Dep't of Educ., Policy Interpretation: Title IX and Intercollegiate Athletics, https://www.ed.gov/laws-and-policy/civil-rights-laws/ federal-register-notices-and-regulations/policy-interpretation-title-ix-and-intercollegiate-athletics.
\12\B.P.J. v. West Virginia No. 24-43, slip op. at 10 (U.S., June 30, 2026).
\13\Id. at 9-12.
H.R. 8781 IS UNNECESSARY TO ``PROTECT'' ATHLETICS
H.R. 8781 would clarify that under Title IX ``sex'' means ``biological'' sex at birth and would also add definitions of ``female'' and ``male'' based on biological sex at birth to Title IX. At first glance, this seems very unnecessary: both the B.P.J. majority opinion written by Justice Kavanaugh and leading dissent written by Justice Sotomayor make clear that all parties in these cases agreed that ``sex'' in Title IX should be interpreted to mean sex assigned at birth.\14\ This was also the interpretation of ``sex'' in the Bostock case which recognized discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity as sex discrimination under title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.\15\ The brief concurrence by Justice Gorsuch suggests his Bostock analysis is still good law: many instances of discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity are outgrowths of underlying discrimination on the basis of sex.\16\
\14\Id. at 10-11; Id. at 30-31 (Sotomayor, J., dissenting).
\15\Id. at 2 (Gorsuch, J., concurring) (``Bostock v. Clayton County supports, not undermines, the Court's conclusion.'') (internal citations omitted); Bostock v. Clayton County, 590 U.S. 644, 660.
\16\Id.
Both the Kavanaugh opinion and Sotomayor dissent provide additional clues as to why the Majority is now advancing H.R. 8781. Justice Kavanaugh, writing for the majority, made two prominent caveats that bookend his opinion. First, very early on, he states that this case does not ``present the distinct question of whether, under Title IX and the equal Protection Clause, schools may allow biological males who identify as female to participate on girls' and women's sports teams. . . . Nothing in this opinion is intended to decide that question.''\17\ He makes it clear the Court in this decision is not stopping a state from allowing or requiring girls' and women's teams to allow transgender girls and women to play. Committee Republicans claim H.R. 8781 is necessary to prevent states and localities from doing just what the Court said it was not outruling: interpreting Title IX to require schools to allow transgender athletes to play on teams consistent with their gender identity. As such, H.R. 8781 seems to contradict the supposed overarching education policy goal of the Majority on this Committee--to return education to the states. The Supreme Court made clear nothing in the B.P.J. ruling prevents a state or locality from recognizing a transgender student's right to be free from discrimination on the basis of their gender identity. In response, the Majority has offered H.R. 8781, nationwide legislation to overrule such an interpretation and take decision-making authority in education away from the states.
\17\B.P.J. v. West Virginia No. 24-43, slip op. at 3 (U.S., June 30, 2026) (n.1).
